chunks: By God, you are not sufficient for me against yourselves,
so how can you be sufficient for me against others?
Before me, the people used to complain of the oppression of their rulers,
and indeed, today I complain of the wrongful actions of my people;
as though I am led by them and they are the leaders,
or that I am the subject and they are the rulers.
ai.seo_question: What is Imam Ali's lament regarding the relationship between rulers and the ruled in Nahj al-Balagha?
ai.summary: In this poignant passage from Nahj al-Balagha, Imam Ali (peace be upon him) articulates the unique burden of leadership during times of internal strife, highlighting the paradox where the ruler becomes subservient to the unruly populace. This lament reflects the historical context of the Battle of the Camel and the subsequent civil unrest, illustrating the spiritual and political exhaustion of a leader who is 'bound' by the very people he is meant to guide. The metaphors of being 'led by the led' and 'ruled by the subjects' underscore the fragility of authority when the ruled lack discipline, a theme deeply resonant in Shia political theology regarding the responsibilities of the Just Ruler.

en.sayed-ali-raza: You cannot be enough for me against yourselves,
so how can you be enough for me against others?
Before me the people used to complain of the oppression of their rulers
but now I have to complain of the wrongful actions of my people;
as though I am led by them and they are the leaders
or that I am the subject and they are the rulers.
